name: Bass music - sub, mid and drum bus chain
description: Reference checklist for the shared mix of dubstep, riddim, deathstep and tearout: a separate mono sub, a mid bass that owns the character, a drum bus with Drum Buss, a kick-keyed sidechain, gain staging with headroom, and a mono check. Not executable.

manual.instruction: Keep the sub on its own track and in mono below about 100 Hz with Utility. Let the mid bass carry all the character, distortion and movement.
manual.verify: Closing one eye at the analyser shows one owner per band: sub below, character above.
manual.why: Every heavy-bass guide splits the clean sub from the distorted mid; a stereo sub is the most common mix fault in the style.

manual.instruction: Group the drums and put one Drum Buss across the group. Use Boom around 30-40 Hz for the kick, Crunch for snares and claps, and the compressor with the input trim setting how hard it works.
manual.verify: The kit sounds like one instrument and the snare cuts without a separate boost.
manual.why: Drum Buss is built for a drum group: its compressor, boom and crunch sections are aimed at exactly these jobs.

manual.instruction: Key a Compressor on the mid bass from the kick, 3-5 dB of gain reduction, and leave the sub layer untouched. Do the same for pads or vocals only if they mask the kick.
manual.verify: Each kick hit is audible without raising the kick's level.
manual.why: Sidechaining the bass rather than boosting the kick keeps the overall level and headroom under control.

manual.instruction: Gain stage so the master peaks around -6 dBFS before any limiter. Put the loudness in the mix, not in the master chain.
manual.verify: The drop is loud in the room while the master meter still has room.
manual.why: These styles are mastered loud; arriving at the master with headroom is what makes that possible without clipping.

manual.instruction: Check the drop in mono. If the growl disappears or the sub drops out, the width is coming from a layer that is cancelling itself.
manual.verify: The drop keeps its weight and its character summed to one speaker.
manual.why: Club systems and phone speakers are effectively mono; stereo width on a bass layer is decoration, not weight.

manual.instruction: A/B the drop against one reference track at the same loudness, not louder. Note which band is emptier in yours: that is the next move, not more compression.
manual.verify: You can name the one band or element that differs from the reference.
manual.why: Loudness-matched comparison is the only comparison that tells you about balance rather than level.

notes: Sources: Bass Kleph's Drum Buss explainer (https://www.basskleph.com/blog/mixing-drums-with-ableton-drum-buss); EDMProd's dubstep drop walkthrough on low-end control and arrangement (https://www.pointblankmusicschool.com/blog/how-to-create-a-dubstep-drop-from-scratch); Ableton's Live Instrument Reference for Utility, Multiband Dynamics and Compressor (https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/live-instrument-reference). Reference-only; it changes nothing by itself.
